  • Why “artificial intelligence” has no single definition, and what the rational-agent definition offers an engineer that the Turing test does not.
  • The sequence McCulloch–Pitts → perceptron → Perceptrons → backpropagation → AlexNet, what each contributed, and why the two winters happened.
  • The difference between knowledge that is programmed (expert systems such as MYCIN) and knowledge that is learned, and why the latter made data the central concern of the field.
  • The four approaches — symbolic, connectionist, statistical, evolutionary — with one medical example each; the difference between an algorithm and a model; the ANI/AGI/ASI tiers and the reactive / limited-memory / theory-of-mind / self-aware taxonomy, and where every system in this course sits (limited memory).
  • What generative AI is (text, image, video), why GPT is generative and BERT is not, and what new failure modes it brings (fluent falsehoods; synthetic media).
  • The five stages of the pattern-recognition pipeline and which two this course concentrates on.
  • The data matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) (\(n \times p\)) and label vector \(\mathbf{y}\); the five data types and why nominal variables must be one-hot encoded.
  • How to turn an image or a signal into a feature vector, and why a pattern is a region of feature space.
  • The nearest-centroid classifier: how it is trained, how it decides, what its decision boundary looks like, and how its accuracy depends on the size of the training sample.
  • The three properties of the training sample (sample ≠ population; labels define the task; size bounds learning) and the failure mode associated with each (dataset shift and shortcuts; label bias; overfitting).
  • Re-identification by quasi-identifiers, k-anonymity, and the Chilean and international rules that govern health data and AI medical devices.

9. Self-assessment

  1. Russell and Norvig’s four definitions of AI differ along two axes. Name them, and say in which quadrant a retinal-screening system belongs and why.
Human versus rational, and thought versus action. A screening system is a rational agent (acting rationally): it perceives an image and acts — outputs a referral decision — so as to maximise a measurable objective; it makes no claim to think like, or appear as, a human.
  1. What did Minsky and Papert prove in 1969, and why did it not prevent today’s neural networks?
That a single-layer perceptron cannot represent functions such as XOR that are not linearly separable. Multi-layer networks can represent them, and backpropagation (1986) made multi-layer networks trainable; what was missing in 1969 was a training algorithm and the compute to run it, not a theoretical possibility.
  1. MYCIN performed at specialist level and was never deployed. Give two reasons, and say which one still applies to AI systems today.
Legal liability for machine recommendations, integration into clinical workflow (interactive sessions took longer than a consult), the computing infrastructure of the 1970s, and the brittleness and maintenance cost of hand-written rules. Liability and workflow integration remain the main barriers today; brittleness has been transformed rather than solved (learned systems are brittle under dataset shift).
  1. In the chunks of Section 3.5, the learned tree (95.5%) agrees with the biopsy more often than the hand-written rule (89.0%). Give two reasons why that comparison is unfair to the hand-written rule.
The tree’s agreement was measured on the same cases it was fitted to, so it is optimistically biased; and the tree searched all nine features and all thresholds while the rule used two features with round-number thresholds. A fair comparison would evaluate both on held-out cases (Supplement S1).
  1. A dataset codes tumour stage as I = 1, II = 2, III = 3, IV = 4 and blood group as O = 1, A = 2, B = 3, AB = 4. Which coding is defensible and which is not, and what should be done instead?
Stage is ordinal, so integer codes preserve the order and are defensible if one accepts equal spacing. Blood group is nominal; the integer coding invents an order and distances. It should be one-hot encoded into four binary columns.
  1. In Figure 5 the 1,000-sample signals were reduced to two features. Name one piece of information lost in that reduction and describe how you would find out whether the loss matters.
The waveform shape of each beat (for example, QRS width or T-wave morphology) is lost; only timing is kept. Whether it matters is decided empirically: train classifiers on both representations and compare their performance on held-out data for the task at hand.
  1. Compute by hand: nearest-centroid classifier with centroids \(\mu_B = (12, 2)\) and \(\mu_M = (19, 9)\); classify \(\mathbf{x} = (16, 6)\).
\(d_B = \sqrt{16 + 16} = \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66\); \(d_M = \sqrt{9 + 9} = \sqrt{18} \approx 4.24\). The case is classified malignant. (It is on the malignant side of the bisector, which passes through the midpoint (15.5, 5.5).)
  1. In Figure 8 the accuracy stops improving after a few dozen training cases. Is this evidence that more data would be useless for this problem?
No. It is evidence that more data would be useless for this classifier, whose straight-line boundary cannot represent the overlap between classes. A more flexible classifier would continue to benefit from more data (and would need it to avoid overfitting).
  1. A hospital releases a dataset with name and identity number removed, keeping date of birth, sex and comuna. Is it anonymised? What is the minimal change that would make it 5-anonymous, and what does that cost?
No; those three quasi-identifiers make most records unique (Section 7.2). Generalising date of birth to year or decade, and possibly comuna to region, until every combination appears at least five times would achieve 5-anonymity, at the cost of age resolution and geographical detail for any downstream model.
  1. In the shortcut-learning simulation, which single number would have revealed the problem before deployment, and why do the training-hospital numbers fail to reveal it?
The accuracy on data from the deployment hospital (external validation). In the training hospital the scanner identifier genuinely predicts the label, so every internal measurement — training accuracy, held-out accuracy from the same hospital — remains high.
  1. The algorithm in Obermeyer et al. used no racial variable. How did racial bias enter it, and what was the remedy?
Through the label: healthcare cost was used as a proxy for health need, and cost is systematically lower for Black patients at the same level of illness. Replacing the cost label by a measure of illness (number of active chronic conditions) reduced the disparity by 84 %.
  1. “The algorithm decided to deny the claim.” Rewrite the sentence using the vocabulary of Section 1.2 and explain what changed.
“A model, produced by a learning algorithm from historical claims data, predicted a high probability of fraud and the system acted on the prediction.” The rewrite makes explicit that the behaviour was learned from data (so the training sample and its label can be examined), that a threshold and an action policy were chosen by people, and that the deployed object is a model, not a procedure.
  1. Deep Blue is classified as “reactive” and a trained spam filter as “limited memory”, yet Deep Blue searched millions of positions and the spam filter only counts words. Why is the filter placed in the higher tier?
The taxonomy sorts by use of the past, not by computational effort. Deep Blue’s evaluation was fixed at design time and it carried nothing from one game to the next; the filter’s parameters were learned from stored past examples and change if it is retrained. Learning from stored experience is what defines the limited-memory tier.
  1. Which of the WHO’s six principles does external validation serve, and which does k-anonymity serve?
External validation serves safety, robustness (well-being and public interest) and, when stratified by subgroup, inclusiveness and equity. k-anonymity serves the protection of autonomy and privacy.

Glossary

Artificial intelligence (AI)
The study and construction of systems that perceive their environment and act so as to achieve their goals; historically, the attempt to make machines perform tasks that require intelligence when performed by people.
Anonymisation / pseudonymisation
Irreversible removal of the link between a record and a person / replacement of identifiers by a code whose key is kept separately (reversible; still personal data under the GDPR).
Classifier
A function that maps a feature vector to a class label or to a probability distribution over classes; its parameters are learned from a training sample.
Connectionism
The approach to AI in which knowledge is stored implicitly in the weights of networks of simple units and acquired by training.
Dataset shift
A difference between the distribution of the training data and that of the data encountered in deployment; the main cause of degraded performance of deployed models.
Deepfake
Synthetic image, audio or video that depicts a real person saying or doing something they did not; produced by generative models.
ELIZA effect
The tendency of users to attribute understanding or intention to a system that merely manipulates symbols; named after Weizenbaum’s 1966 chatbot.
Expert system
A symbolic AI program that encodes the knowledge of a human expert as rules and reasons with them; MYCIN is the medical prototype.
Generative AI
Models trained on large collections of content that produce new content of the same kind (text, images, video, molecules); large language models and diffusion models are the main families.
Feature / feature vector
A measured or computed property of an object / the fixed-length vector of all such properties that represents the object to the classifier.
k-anonymity
The property of a dataset in which every combination of quasi-identifier values is shared by at least k records.
Label (target, response)
The known class or value associated with each training object; what the classifier learns to predict.
Machine learning
The sub-field of AI in which a system’s behaviour is learned from data rather than programmed.
Model vs algorithm
An algorithm is a fixed procedure; a model is an object with parameters learned from data by a learning algorithm. The model is what is deployed.
Nearest-centroid classifier
The classifier that assigns an object to the class whose mean feature vector is closest; its decision boundaries are hyperplanes.
Nominal / ordinal / continuous
Data types: unordered categories / ordered categories without fixed spacing / real-valued measurements. The type determines the admissible operations.
One-hot encoding
Representation of a nominal variable with k levels as k binary indicator columns, so that no order or distance between levels is implied.
Pattern recognition
The discipline concerned with the automatic classification of objects (images, signals, measurements) into categories.
Perceptron
Rosenblatt’s 1958 learning machine: a threshold unit whose weights are adjusted from labelled examples; the ancestor of neural networks.
Quasi-identifier
An attribute that is not an identifier by itself but, combined with others, can single out a person (date of birth, sex, postal code).
Rational agent
A system that perceives through sensors and acts through actuators so as to maximise the expected achievement of its objective; the working definition of AI in modern textbooks.
Shortcut learning
A model’s reliance on a spurious regularity of the training data (such as a hospital marker) that predicts the label there but not elsewhere.
Training sample (training set)
The labelled data from which a classifier’s parameters are learned; a sample from, not the whole of, the population the classifier will be applied to.

Textbooks

  • Russell S, Norvig P. Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach. 4th ed. Pearson; 2021. — Chapters 1–2 for the definitions and history of this unit; the standard reference of the field.
  • Bishop CM. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer; 2006. — Chapter 1 for the statistical view of pattern recognition. Free PDF from the author’s site.
  • Duda RO, Hart PE, Stork DG. Pattern Classification. 2nd ed. Wiley; 2001. — The classic pattern-recognition text; Chapter 1 defines the pipeline of Section 4.2.
  • James G, Witten D, Hastie T, Tibshirani R. An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R. 2nd ed. Springer; 2021. — The R companion to the whole course; free PDF at statlearning.com.
  • Venables WN, Ripley BD. Modern Applied Statistics with S (MASS). 4th ed. Springer; 2002. — The reference for the R modelling functions used throughout this edition.
  • Topol EJ. High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence. Nat Med. 2019;25:44–56. — A readable survey of medical applications and their evidence base.

Online resources

  • mlbench package documentation — cran.r-project.org/package=mlbench; the breast-cancer and other benchmark datasets used in this course.
  • UCI Machine Learning Repository — archive.ics.uci.edu; original source of the breast-cancer and digits data.
  • Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, Ley Chile — bcn.cl/leychile; consolidated texts of Laws 19.628, 20.584 and 21.719.
  • FDA, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Software as a Medical Device — fda.gov.
  • WHO guidance on ethics and governance of AI for health — who.int.
Study material for BGM-411 Inteligencia Artificial (R edition), Universidad Católica del Maule. This page was knitted from the R-Markdown source U1.Rmd; every figure and number was produced by the R code shown, and the notebook runs in Google Colab (R runtime). Last built 18 October 2026.
